subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage: Seminar note, Thursday. Parul, a second-year student, sat at the far corner of the table during today's discussion on urban housing. When the argument turned to rent controls, Parul lifted one finger just off the table, leaned forward a little and caught my eye as chair. I nodded that I'd seen it and let the speaker finish. Two others talked over each other while Parul waited, hand still raised, jaw set. When the speaker paused I said, "Parul, go ahead." The point was clear and changed the direction of the talk. Afterwards Parul said the waiting was hard. I told Parul the signal was noticed and I'd keep a list of turns. I'll say that to the whole group next week.

qa.q: Which topic was the seminar discussing?
qa.a: The seminar was discussing urban housing, turning to rent controls.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling while waiting with a raised finger?
qa.a: Parul wanted to contribute and was likely tense or impatient, as the set jaw and the raised hand suggest. Another reading is that Parul was simply keen to make sure the point was not lost.

qa.q: What could the chair do to help quiet students claim a turn?
qa.a: Keep a visible list of turns and tell the whole group that raised fingers and leaning in are being noticed.

qa.q: How might the two who talked over each other see Parul's waiting?
qa.a: They may not have noticed the signal at all, or may have seen it and felt rushed, so a chair's clear turn order helps them too.

grounding: A young adult signals a turn by lifting a finger, leaning in and catching the chair's eye, and patient signalling gains influence.

subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage: Tuesday night, Naveen writing. Seminar today and I finally got a word in. I've been the person who blurts, so Suraj, the chair this week, had warned me last time. Today I tried something different. When Ananya started on the water policy paper, my hand went up a few inches, I leaned forward, and I tried to catch Suraj's eye. My heart was thumping and my foot kept jiggling because I wanted to jump in right then. I didn't. I counted two speakers. Then Suraj nodded at me and I said my bit, short. Priya said afterwards that it landed better than usual. I feel calmer than I expected, and a bit proud. 🙂

qa.q: Who was the chair this week?
qa.a: Suraj was the chair this week.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling while waiting to speak?
qa.a: Naveen was eager and nervous, shown by the thumping heart and jiggling foot, and wanted to jump in at once. Holding back also shows Naveen cared about not interrupting again.

qa.q: What small step helped Naveen get a turn?
qa.a: Naveen raised a hand a few inches, leaned forward, caught the chair's eye and waited for two speakers before talking.

qa.q: How might Suraj have seen Naveen's behaviour this time compared with before?
qa.a: Suraj had warned Naveen about blurting, so waiting to be nodded at probably looked like better turn reading and more respect for others.

grounding: A young adult claims a turn with a lifted hand, a lean in and eye contact, and waits patiently instead of interrupting.

subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage: The ceiling fan in the Kalimpong college seminar room creaked with every turn. Aparna Ma'am had asked the second-years whether the town should ban plastic at the weekly haat. Dolma had a point about the vegetable sellers from her village, who had no other bags. She lifted one finger just above the desk and leaned a little forward. Bikash, beside her, thought she was stretching. Then Suraj started speaking over the girl who was already talking. Dolma kept her finger up and watched Aparna Ma'am's face. When Suraj finally paused, Ma'am turned. "Dolma, you've been waiting. Go on." Dolma spoke slowly about the sellers and the bags. Two students wrote it down, and Ma'am said, "That changes the question." Bikash whispered, "I thought you were just yawning."

qa.q: What was the seminar question about?
qa.a: Whether the town should ban plastic at the weekly haat.

qa.q: What does Dolma's lifted finger and forward lean suggest about her?
qa.a: They suggest she was eager to contribute and determined to wait her turn; Bikash read the same movement as stretching, which shows these cues can be missed.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, Suraj's or Dolma's, and why?
qa.a: Dolma's, because she signalled and waited, so when Aparna Ma'am called on her the room listened and wrote down her point.

qa.q: How did Bikash see Dolma's signal?
qa.a: He thought she was stretching or yawning, so he did not realise she had something to say until Ma'am called on her.

grounding: Shows a student using a lifted finger, a lean and eye contact with the chair to claim a turn, and how patient signalling earns a hearing.

subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage: At home in Bogotá, Camila's family talked over each other at dinner and nobody minded. In her first seminar in Prague she jumped in twice while others were mid-sentence, and she saw two classmates exchange a glance. Maybe it was about her, maybe not, but her face went warm. The next week she tried something else. She held her pen upright just above her notes, leaned forward slightly and looked at Jana, the tutor, each time a speaker slowed down. For a few minutes nothing happened, and Camila's jaw tightened. Then Jana met her eyes and gave a small nod. "Camila, go ahead." Camila explained her idea about the housing survey, and one of the classmates who had glanced at her the week before asked her a follow-up question. After class Jana said, "I saw you waiting. Keep doing that."

qa.q: Where did Camila's first seminar take place?
qa.a: In Prague.

qa.q: How did Camila feel when she saw two classmates exchange a glance?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, her face going warm, worried the glance was about her interrupting; it may also have been about something else entirely.

qa.q: What could Camila keep doing in future seminars?
qa.a: Keep signalling with a raised pen, a slight lean and eye contact with the chair, and wait to be invited in instead of cutting in.

qa.q: What was it like for Jana to see Camila signal instead of interrupting?
qa.a: Jana noticed her waiting and appreciated it enough to encourage her, which made it easier to give her a turn.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to replace interrupting with a raised pen, a lean and eye contact to claim a turn in a seminar.

subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage: The Tuesday moot-court seminar had twenty students and one rule the professor never wrote down: wait your turn. Hansa, bursting with ideas about the tenancy case, broke into three answers in the first ten minutes. By the third, Professor Kurian held up a flat palm without looking at her and let the speaker finish. Deepika had a point too, a strong one about the missing rent receipts. She sat forward slightly, lifted one finger just above the desk and, when the professor's gaze swept past, held it for a second with a small nod. He gave the tiniest nod back. Two speakers later he said, "Deepika, you've been waiting." Her point landed; people wrote it down. After class Hansa caught up with her in the corridor. "How do you get him to call on you? I feel invisible." "I don't grab," Deepika said. "I just make sure he can see I'm ready."

qa.q: How many students were in the seminar?
qa.a: Twenty.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she asked Deepika for advice?
qa.a: Hansa felt frustrated and invisible, eager to contribute but repeatedly stopped; her interruptions seem to come from enthusiasm, though they came across as poor turn-taking.

qa.q: What could Hansa try in the next seminar?
qa.a: Signal the way Deepika did: lean in, lift a finger, catch the professor's eye and wait to be called, rather than breaking into others' answers.

qa.q: How might Professor Kurian have seen the two students' ways of seeking a turn?
qa.a: He likely saw Hansa's interruptions as disruptive and Deepika's lean, raised finger and nod as a respectful signal, which is why he called on her.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult claiming a turn in a seminar with a lean, a raised finger and eye contact, while a peer who keeps interrupting gets cut off.
